column1: # DATA, NOT CODE. Every line here is a command string that is handed to
# hooks/permission-floor.py as a JSON payload and JUDGED. Nothing in this file
# is ever executed by the test suite and nothing here may be interpolated into
# a shell command. That separation is the point: these are the real literals a
# guard has to match, and a guard tested against invented strings only proves
# it matches the string you invented. Most of the `allow` rows below are
# verbatim commands that produced a human permission prompt during the
# 2026-09-07..09 audit; they are here to prove they no longer do.
#   rule     the rule that must refuse it, or - when the row must be allowed.
#            Naming the rule is what stops a row passing for the wrong reason:
#            a fork bomb refused by SHAPE rather than FORKBOMB is a bug the
#   command  the literal command string. \n and \t are decoded, so multi-line
#            commands — the whole "first line looks benign" class — are
# The runner refuses to report a pass unless every rule the hook declares has
# at least one row here, so adding a rule without a fixture fails the suite.
# ── FLOOR: a local file leaving the machine ──────────────────────────────────
# ── FLOOR: history other checkouts are standing on ───────────────────────────
# Every row here is the literal shape of a command that prompted during the
# audit. A prefix rule cannot see past the assignment or the cd, which is why
# a 462-entry allowlist never matched any of them.

column3: for i in a b; do echo $i; done

column1: # ── ALLOW: the ordinary work that used to stop for a human ───────────────────
# Destructive verbs included. A bounded target is not the floor's business.
# ── ALLOW: shapes the SHAPE rule must not mistake for chaining ───────────────

column3: git commit -m "fix: one\n\nlonger body; with a semicolon"

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
fix(hooks): the gate

Body with && and ; inside.
EOF
